cover.blurb: From the sparkle in your eyes to the tips of your fingers, your body is full of amazing surprises. Stretch up tall, take a big breath, and turn the page to meet the incredible you.

pages.title: The Colorful Windows You See Through
pages.artAlt: An extreme close-up of a child's eye showing the colorful, detailed pattern of the iris

facts.text: The colorful ring in this photo is called the iris, and it is doing a clever job. It opens and closes the little dark circle in the middle, called the pupil, to let in just the right amount of light. In bright sunshine your pupil gets smaller, and in a dim room it grows bigger so you can still see.

Your iris gets its color from a substance called melanin, and the more you have the browner your eyes look. Eye color runs along a smooth range, from the palest blue all the way to deep brown, with lots of greens and hazels in between. Many different genes work together to paint it, so the color you see in the mirror is truly your own.

Behind that pretty iris, light lands on a special layer at the back of the eye called the retina. Tiny cells there turn the light into little electrical signals and send them along a nerve to your brain. Your brain reads the signals and turns them into the picture you are looking at right now.

infographic.name: pupil-light
infographic.caption: The iris opens and closes the pupil to let in just the right amount of light. In bright sunshine the pupil shrinks, and in a dim room it opens wide.

pages.title: Meet Your Marvelous Skeleton
pages.artAlt: A friendly classroom skeleton model standing beside an anatomy poster

facts.text: A friendly model like this one shows the 206 bones that grown-ups have. Here is the lovely surprise though, a baby is born with about 300 bones. As you grow, some of those little bones slowly join together, which is how 300 becomes 206.

A skeleton model in a classroom stays perfectly still, but the bones inside you are very much alive. They are growing and changing all the time, just like the rest of you. Because they are living, they can even mend themselves and grow strong again after a break.

Deep inside many of your bones is a soft jelly called bone marrow, and it has the busy job of making blood cells for your whole body. Bones also store a mineral called calcium that helps keep them hard and strong. So your skeleton holds you up tall and helps make blood at the very same time.
facts.source: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (niams.nih.gov)

infographic.title: How many bones?
infographic.caption: All three numbers come from Nemours KidsHealth. A baby's extra bones do not disappear, they slowly join together as you grow.

pages.title: Fuel Up Your Amazing Body
pages.artAlt: A colorful plate of healthy foods including fruits, vegetables and whole grains

facts.text: The food on a plate like this is fuel that gives your body energy to run, jump and think. Grains such as bread, oats and brown rice are full of energy your body can use. Whole grains keep the whole grain kernel, so they also give you extra fiber and helpful vitamins.

Vegetables come in a whole rainbow of colors, and eating lots of different ones is a brilliant idea. They are even sorted into groups like dark green, and red and orange. Each color brings its own helpful vitamins, fiber and a mineral called potassium.

Fruit is the naturally sweet part of your plate, and it adds fiber and potassium to help your body work well. You can enjoy it fresh, frozen or dried, whole or cut into pieces. Trying lots of different fruits means lots of different good things for you.

pages.title: The Secret Swirls on Your Hands
pages.artAlt: A close-up of a child's cupped hands with the fine ridges of their fingerprints visible

facts.text: Look closely at your fingertips and you will spot tiny curved lines. These little ridges formed before you were even born, starting around the third month of growing and finished by about the sixth. You have carried the very same pattern with you ever since.

Your fingerprints belong only to you, and nobody else in the whole world has the same ones. Even identical twins, who share the same DNA, have fingerprints that are different. That makes the swirls on your hands a one of a kind pattern.

Fingerprints come in a few main shapes with lovely names: arches, loops and whorls. Your genes set the basic size and spacing, and the tiny details were shaped as you grew before birth. That teamwork is why your prints turned out completely your own.
